speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Hello everyone, welcome to lecture three of Introduction to Machine Learning.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Today we finally open the black box and look at how a model actually learns.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: We start with a neural network: layers of tiny units that each multiply, add and pass a number on.

speaker: Sara
text: Are those units like real brain cells?

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Loosely inspired by them, but much simpler. Think of them as adjustable dials.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Every dial is a parameter, and a modern model can have billions of them.

speaker: Yanis
text: How does the model know which way to turn the dials?

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: First we need a training set: thousands of examples where we already know the right answer.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Then a loss function measures how wrong the model is on those examples.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: The goal of learning is simply to make that number as small as possible.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: We do it with gradient descent: we nudge every parameter a little in the direction that reduces the loss.

speaker: Sara
text: And how do we know that direction for billions of parameters?

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Backpropagation computes it efficiently, starting from the error and working backwards through the layers.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: {listener}, what do you think happens if we nudge the parameters too much at each step?

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Exactly, it overshoots. That step size is called the learning rate.

speaker: Yanis
text: So small steps are always better?

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Too small and training takes forever. One full pass over the training set is called an epoch, and we often need dozens.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Now the classic trap: overfitting.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: The model memorises the training examples instead of learning the general pattern.

speaker: Sara
text: Like a student who memorises last year's exam answers?

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Perfect analogy. It does great on familiar questions and fails on new ones.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: That's why we keep a separate test set the model never sees during training.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: To fight it we also use regularization, which penalises overly complicated models.

speaker: Yanis
text: Does all this apply to chat assistants too?

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Yes. They're built on the transformer, a network design that pays attention to every word in relation to the others.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Same recipe though: a loss, gradient descent, and an enormous training set.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: {listener}, could you explain in your own words the difference between the training set and the test set?

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: Very clear, thank you. For next week, try the gradient descent notebook on the course page.

speaker: Dr. Nguyen
text: See you on Tuesday.
